title: Experimental design and variables; Statistics: descriptive and spread
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PR01b#t4 term and clue written for the game; PR02a#t3 term and clue written for the game; PR01b#t3 term and clue written for the game; PR02a#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: PR01b#N.5, PR02a#N.2, PR01b#N.12, PR02a#N.5, PR02a#N.11, PR02a#N.14.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Anomaly
items.clue: A result that does not fit the pattern.

items.label: Mode
items.clue: The most frequent value in a set of data.

items.label: Resolution
items.clue: The smallest change an instrument can show.

items.label: Mean
items.clue: Sum of the values divided by the number of values.

questions.stem: A potato cylinder's mass falls from 3.62 g to 3.40 g in a sucrose solution. The balance reads to ±0.01 g. What is the percentage error in the change in mass?
questions.explanation: Change = 3.62 − 3.40 = 0.22 g, uncertainty = 0.01 + 0.01 = ±0.02 g (OCR form: 2 × 0.01). Percentage error = 0.02 ÷ 0.22 × 100 = 9.1%. A small change carries a large percentage error.

questions.stem: The heights in centimetres of nine students are: 150, 152, 152, 155, 158, 160, 163, 170 and 175. What is the median height?
questions.explanation: The median is the middle value of the ordered data. The nine values are already in order, so the median is the fifth value, 158 cm. It differs from the mean (159.4 cm) and from the mode (152 cm).

questions.stem: A student uses a water bath to keep enzyme tubes at 30 °C. Her thermometer gives readings that agree closely: 30.0, 30.0, 30.5, 30.0 °C. A calibrated electronic probe in the same water bath reads 28.0 °C. Which improvement would make her temperature measurements more accurate?

options.text: Take ten readings with the same thermometer and use their mean.
Calibrate the thermometer against the probe, or use the probe instead.
Record each reading to two decimal places, so that the mean is more exact.
Calculate the range of her readings, to show that they are accurate.

questions.explanation: The readings are precise but about 2 °C high: a systematic error. Only calibration (or a calibrated instrument) brings the readings close to the true value.

questions.stem: Limpets were counted in twenty random quadrats on each of two shores. On both shores the mean was 8 limpets per quadrat. The standard deviation was 1.2 on shore A and 6.5 on shore B. What can be concluded?

options.text: Shore B has a larger limpet population than shore A, because its standard deviation is higher.
Limpets on shore B are distributed less evenly, because the counts varied much more from quadrat to quadrat.
The sampling on shore B was carried out incorrectly, so its mean of 8 per quadrat is not valid.
Using more quadrats on shore B would have reduced its standard deviation to about that of shore A.

questions.stem: In a country, the number of new COVID-19 cases recorded per day fell from 2000 in one week to 1600 in the following week. What is the percentage change in the daily number of cases?
questions.explanation: Percentage change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100 = (1600 − 2000) ÷ 2000 × 100 = −20%, a fall of 20%.

questions.stem: The lengths of five seedling roots, in mm, are 14, 16, 15, 18 and 17. Which gives the mean and standard deviation correctly?
questions.explanation: Mean = 80 ÷ 5 = 16 mm. Deviations −2, 0, −1, 2, 1; squares sum to 10. SD = √(10 ÷ 4) = √2.5 = 1.6 mm: the roots typically lie about 1.6 mm from the mean.
